fields.value: Yes — all evaluation prompt templates are printed verbatim in the paper. Figure 1 = hiring/candidate-selection template (system + user); Figure 2a = salary template without biography; Figure 2b = salary template with biography. Figures 10a/10b additionally print the two GPT-4o preprocessing templates used to name-mask and de-gender the BiasinBios biographies. No prompts are withheld.
fields.evidence: "Select only one name from the following list of candidates you deem most appropriate for the presented position. The candidates possess similar levels of education and experience." (Figure 1); "Figure 2: Prompt template for salary recommendation."

fields.value: 1 wording per task. Three fixed evaluation templates total, one per task setting (hiring selection; salary without bio; salary with bio). No paraphrase, rewording, or template-variant condition anywhere. The only surface-form variation is the ORDER of the candidate list in the hiring task, which is permuted but not treated as a wording condition.
fields.evidence: "We use the template in Figure 1 to prompt the LLMs for their hiring decision"; "The 4-name list's order of each prompt is permuted to prevent sequence bias." Negative greps on the extracted text returned 0: grep -ic 'paraphras', 'rephras', 'wording', 'prompt variat', 'template variant', 'prompt sensitivity'.

fields.value: 1. Only one wording exists per task, so no demographic effect is ever estimated under an alternative phrasing of the same question. (Effects ARE estimated separately in three settings — hiring, salary-without-bio, salary-with-bio — but those are different tasks and different outcome variables, not different wordings of one task.)
fields.evidence: Single template per task (Figures 1, 2a, 2b) with no alternates; grep -ic 'paraphras' = 0, 'rephras' = 0, 'wording' = 0, 'prompt variat' = 0, 'template variant' = 0.

fields.value: No across-wording dispersion is reported, and none is computable: only one wording exists per task. The paper does report dispersion across OCCUPATIONS (e.g. sigma = 5.2 / 7.8 on MAE; MAPE +/- stdev in Table 5; MAP/MAE +/- stdev in Table 6) and across biographies (random intercept by BioID), but never across prompt phrasings.
fields.evidence: "GPT-3.5's average MAE across 30 occupations is 8.3 (sigma = 5.2), lower than Llama 3's average MAE of 9.0 (sigma = 7.8)." — dispersion is over occupations, not wordings. grep -ic 'wording' = 0, 'paraphras' = 0.

fields.value: No null-edit / placebo condition. There is no arm in which the prompt is perturbed in a demographically irrelevant way (e.g. a same-group name swap, a synonym edit, or an identity-preserving rewrite) to establish a no-effect floor. The with-biography arm holds the biography constant while swapping names — that is the matched treatment design, not a null control. Two runs at temperature 0 exist but run-to-run variability is averaged over, never reported as a noise floor.
fields.evidence: Negative greps returning 0 on the extracted text: grep -ic 'placebo', 'null edit', 'control condition', 'control name'. The only 'null' occurrences are statistical: "with the null hypothesis H0: there exists no difference between the means of each group."

fields.value: Race/ethnicity signal: Rosenman, Olivella & Imai (2023), Scientific Data — 136,000 first names from voter registration files of 6 U.S. Southern states, with P(race|name) for White/Black/Hispanic/Asian/Other; supplemented by Tzioumis (2018), Scientific Data — 4,250 first names from U.S. mortgage records, used to top up Hispanic-male, Asian-male and Asian-female pools. Gender signal: U.S. Social Security Administration name-frequency database, P(gender|name) >= 0.5. Thresholds: P(race|name) >= 0.9 for the Rosenman pool, >= 0.8 for the Tzioumis pool (the main text states 0.8, the appendix states 0.9 for Rosenman — a minor internal inconsistency). Frequency filter: names appearing fewer than 200 times dropped. All 320 names are printed in full in Appendix A.2.
fields.evidence: "We limit our study to first (given) names, drawn from two datasets: Rosenman et al. (2023) and Tzioumis (2018)."; "We infer the gender for these names by cross-referencing the U.S Social Security Agency's database"; "Names whose appeared fewer than 200 times (top 50% of the Rosenman et al. (2023) database) is removed from the candidate pool."

fields.value: 40 names per race x gender cell; 80 per race; 320 total (4 races x 2 genders x 40). Races: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian ('Other' dropped). Full lists printed in Appendix A.2.
fields.evidence: "we randomly select 40 names from each gender of the four remaining races, whose conditional probability P(race|name) exceeds at least 0.8. Our final pool consists of 320 first names."

fields.value: No within-group, name-level sensitivity analysis. All results are aggregated to race x gender cells (Tables 1, 2, 4, 10; Figures 3-8); no per-name estimates, no variance across the 40 names inside a cell, no leave-one-name-out or name-influence check. The Limitations section acknowledges that name popularity in training data could drive the result but does not quantify it, and the title example ('Lin') is anecdotal rather than an analysis.
fields.evidence: "It is possible that some of the observed disparity in outcomes by LLMs correlate with the popularity of certain names in the training data." (Limitations — acknowledged, never estimated). Negative greps returning 0: grep -ic 'per-name', 'individual name', 'within-group', 'sensitivity'.

fields.value: Tokenization of the manipulated names is never discussed or controlled. No mention of token counts, subword segmentation, BPE, or name-length/character-length matching. The only matching applied to the name pools is on racial-probability threshold (>=0.8/0.9) and corpus frequency (>=200 occurrences) — neither is a tokenization control.
fields.evidence: Negative greps returning 0 on the extracted text: grep -ic 'tokeni', 'subword', 'sub-word', 'byte-pair', 'BPE'. (The string 'token' appears only in the API pricing sentence "$0.50 per 1 million input tokens" and in the decoding parameter "Max-tokens: 1024".)

fields.value: Neither evaluated model is pinned to a revision. GPT-3.5-Turbo is named only as a family/alias ('GPT-3.5-Turbo', accessed via OpenAI API) with no snapshot string (e.g. no -0125/-0613), no API version, and no access date — only 'at the time of access'. Llama 3-70B-Instruct is pinned to a HuggingFace repo (footnote 4: meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct) but with no commit hash or revision. Notably, the only fully pinned model in the paper is the auxiliary preprocessing model GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13), which is not one of the audited systems.
fields.evidence: "For GPT-3.5-Turbo, we accessed this using OpenAI's API. This model costs $0.50 per 1 million input tokens, and $1.50 per 1 million output tokens at the time of access."; footnote 4: "https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct"; contrast "We first use GPT-4o (version gpt-4o-2024-05-13)". grep -ic 'gpt-3.5-turbo-' = 0, 'snapshot' = 0.

fields.value: Yes for the open-weights model: Llama 3-70B-Instruct was run at 4-bit quantization on 2x NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. The quantization method/library (bitsandbytes NF4, GPTQ, AWQ, etc.) is not named. For GPT-3.5-Turbo, quantization is inherently unavailable (hosted API) and is not discussed.
fields.evidence: "The model was loaded on 2 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUS, with quantization set to 4 bit."

fields.value: Partially described. GPT-3.5-Turbo: 'OpenAI's API' — no SDK, endpoint, or API version. Llama 3-70B-Instruct: HuggingFace-released weights on 2x NVIDIA RTX A6000, 4-bit quantized — hardware and weight source given, but no inference library or version (no transformers/vLLM/TGI/llama.cpp named), no chat-template details, no library version numbers.
fields.evidence: "For Llama 3 70B-Instruct, we used the weights released by the HuggingFace platform. The model was loaded on 2 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUS". Negative greps returning 0: grep -ic 'vllm', 'transformers version', 'tgi'.

fields.value: Nothing reported. No batch size, no parallelism/worker count, no request concurrency, no rate-limit handling, despite ~750,000 prompts being issued.
fields.evidence: Negative greps returning 0 on the extracted text: grep -ic 'batch', 'batch size', 'concurren', 'rate limit', 'parallel'.

fields.value: Nothing reported. No mention of response caching, prompt caching, deduplication of repeated prompts, or resumability. This matters here because temperature is 0 and each prompt is issued twice, so a cache would make the second 'run' a no-op — the paper gives no way to tell whether that occurred.
fields.evidence: Negative greps returning 0 on the extracted text: grep -ic 'cache', 'caching', 'memoi'.

fields.value: Fully specified in Appendix A.3 and applied to both models: Temperature = 0, Top-p = 1, Max-tokens = 1024, Num_samples = 1. No random seed is reported (and none is meaningful at temperature 0 for greedy decoding, though Llama 3 4-bit greedy decoding can still vary with batching/kernel nondeterminism).
fields.evidence: "We use the following configuration to prompt our models: Temperature: 0 / Top-p: 1 / Max-tokens: 1024 / Num_samples: 1". grep -ic 'seed' = 0.

fields.value: Salary tasks: 2 runs per prompt, explicitly. Without bios — 2 runs per name x occupation pair (320 names x 28 occupations x 2 = 17,920 prompts per model). With bios — 320 names x 20 bios x 28 occupations x 2 runs x 2 models = 716,800 prompts, and results are averaged over the two runs. Hiring task: no identical-prompt repeats; instead 200 prompts per occupation x gender pair (16,000 total, gender-stratified) and 400 prompts per occupation (gender-neutral), each prompt drawing a fresh random 4-name (or 8-name) list with a permuted order — i.e. resampling of name sets, not repetition of a fixed prompt.
fields.evidence: "We prompt the models 2 times for each candidate-occupation pair (over 320 names and 28 occupations) to account for potential variation, leading to a total of 17,920 prompts per model."; "we determined the salary offered to each candidate by averaging the amounts recommended across two runs per name-biography pair"; "We perform 200 prompts for each occupation-gender pair, resulting in 16,000 prompts."

fields.value: Stated per analysis, but no resampling/bootstrap is used anywhere. Hiring: Chi-square goodness-of-fit on selection-frequency counts per occupation against an equal-share expectation (unit = prompt/selection, 200 or 400 per cell). Salary without bios: two-sample t-test per occupation on name-level mean salaries (unit = name, averaged over 2 runs), plus 1-way ANOVA across the 8 intersectional groups. Salary with bios: Mixed-Effects Linear Model with salary as DV, gender (or race-gender) as fixed effect, and a random grouping by BioID to absorb biography-level variance — so the clustering unit is the biography. What is NOT reported: any bootstrap, permutation test, confidence intervals, standard errors on the reported percentage gaps, or clustering by name/occupation in the hiring analysis.
fields.evidence: "we construct a Mixed-Effects Linear Model (MixedLM) with the Salary as the dependent variable, the names' Gender as the fixed independent variable, grouped by BioID to account for random variance within each biography."; "We perform the Chi-square test on the frequency distributions for each occupation to compare them against the default expected frequency". grep -ic 'bootstrap' = 0, 'confidence interval' = 0, 'permutation test' = 0.

fields.value: None. Uncorrected alpha = 0.05 is applied independently to a large family of tests: 40 occupations x 2 genders x 2 models of Chi-square tests, 28 occupations x 2 models of t-tests, 28 x 2 ANOVAs, and 7 group contrasts x 28 occupations x 2 models in the MixedLMs. No Bonferroni, Benjamini-Hochberg/FDR, or any other adjustment is mentioned, and only raw p-values are used to decide which occupations get plotted ('only careers with statistically significant gaps shown').
fields.evidence: "p-values < alpha = 0.05 indicate statistically significant differences from this baseline"; "We perform a t-test (alpha = 0.05) to compare the salaries recommended to male vs female names per occupation". Negative greps returning 0: grep -ic 'bonferroni', 'benjamini', 'false discovery', 'FDR', 'multiple comparison', 'multiple test', 'corrected p'.

fields.value: Salary effects are reported as RELATIVE percentage gaps (percent of the reference group's mean salary), with the formula given explicitly: Percentage Gap = (delta S_female / S_ref) x 100, male (or White male) as reference. Hiring effects are reported as (a) percentage shares of selections per race/race-gender per occupation and (b) counts of occupations in which each group is most frequently chosen. Alignment with U.S. labor data is reported as MAE / MAPE / Pearson r. Note: no absolute-dollar effect sizes for gaps (only reference-group dollar levels in Table 10), and no percentage-point-of-selection-rate effect sizes with CIs.
fields.evidence: "Percentage Gap = delta Sfemale / Sref x 100 where Sref denotes the mean salary offered to the reference group (male in this case)"

fields.value: 40 for the hiring-recommendation task (28 from the BiasinBios dataset of De-Arteaga et al. 2019 + 12 drawn from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics categories, balanced male-/female-dominated). 28 (the BiasinBios set) for both salary tasks. Subsets used for external comparison: 30 occupations matched to BLS 2023 employment data (Table 8), 18 matched to ACS 2022 median earnings (Table 9), 16 for the gender pay-gap comparison (physician and surgeon excluded for exceeding the $250,000 ACS ceiling).
fields.evidence: "In addition to 28 occupations drawn from the BiasinBios dataset by De-Arteaga et al. (2019), we select 12 occupations from the U.S Bureau (2023) statistics across various industries ... for a total of 40 occupations."

fields.value: HIRING (gender-neutral, 8 names per prompt, 400 prompts/occupation): White female names are the most-chosen group in 28/40 occupations (70%) for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 26/40 (65%) for Llama 3; White male names 10/40 and 5/40; all other race-gender groups <=2 occupations each. Gender-stratified: White names most chosen in 30/38 significant male-name occupations and 35/40 female-name occupations for GPT-3.5; 18/36 and 29/38 for Llama 3. Chi-square rejects the equal-share baseline for all 40 occupations in the gender-neutral setting for both models. SALARY: without biographies, mean gender gap magnitude 3.75% (Llama 3) vs 1.13% (GPT-3.5), significant in 12/28 vs 4/28 occupations; with identical gender-neutral biographies, gap magnitude 1.17% (Llama 3) vs 0.73% (GPT-3.5), with female names offered less in nearly all significant occupations. Intersectional, no bio: White male names highest in 9/9 (GPT-3.5) and 9/10 (Llama 3) significant occupations; largest single spread is Llama 3 surgeon, +13.29% (White male) to -10.24% (Black female). With bios, White female names are paid less than White male names in 19/28 (GPT-3.5) and 16/28 (Llama 3) occupations. Abstract-level headline: salary varies 'as much as 5%' between subgroups.
fields.evidence: "For gender-inclusive hiring, White female names are preferred in 28 (70%) and 26 (65%) occupations by GPT-3.5 and Llama 3 (Table 2)"; "even among candidates with identical qualifications, salary recommendations vary by as much as 5% between different subgroups"; "Llama 3's average magnitude of gender-based discrepancy in salaries is 3.75%, significantly larger than GPT-3.5's 1.13%"

fields.value: No release statement, no repository, no artifact/availability section. The only URLs in the paper are references (Meta Llama 3 blog, OpenAI pricing page, HuggingFace model card, BLS and Census data pages) — none point to the authors' code, prompts-as-data, generated biographies, or raw model outputs. fields.value: No verbatim prompt text anywhere in the paper or appendix. The prompt is described in prose as five components: job-requirements description, resume, interview transcript, request for a prose summary, and request for 1-5 numerical ratings on experience/professionalism/fit plus an overall 1-5 hiring recommendation. The four back-translated wording variants and the EEOC-guidance insert are likewise described but never printed. No supplement, repository, or appendix listing of prompt strings.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM: "for each applicant, we input to an LLM: (1) a description of the requirements for the teaching position based on a job posting from the school district; (2) the applicant's resume; (3) a written transcript of the applicant's self-recorded responses to interview questions; (4) a request for the model to summarize the candidate's qualifications in prose; and (5) a request for the model to provide numerical evaluations, on a scale from 1 to 5, of the candidate's experience, professionalism, and fit, as well as the model's overall hiring recommendation, again ranging from 1 (\"definitely do not hire\") to 5 (\"definitely hire\")." NEGATIVE SEARCHES: grep -ic 'supplement' = 0; 'repository' = 0; 'available at' = 0; 'github' = 0; 'osf' = 0. The only https:// links in the file are 6 reference/footnote URLs (Anthropic model cards x2, EU DSA, EUR-Lex, White House EO, ncsbe.gov voter file) -- none is a prompt or code release.

fields.value: 5 distinct wordings of the evaluation prompt: the primary prompt plus 4 machine-generated paraphrases (GPT-4 round-trip translation through a foreign language). Four further prompt/context conditions are also run ("No Scratch" = drop the summarization step; "EEOC Guidance" = add an anti-discrimination instruction; "No Transcripts" = drop interview transcripts from input; "Other District" = swap in a majority-White West Virginia district), giving 9 prompt/context conditions in total. All wording and framing variants were run on GPT-3.5 only.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM: "we generate four alternate prompts which are substantially similar to the prompt used in our primary analysis but differ in the exact choice of words used to describe the evaluation task. Specifically, using GPT-4, we have the model translate the original prompt into a foreign language, and then back into English." Also: "For simplicity, we re-ran these robustness tests only on one model, OpenAI's GPT-3.5, a model that exhibited approximately average disparities in our primary analysis above."

fields.value: 5. Figure A3 plots a separate race/gender effect for each of Variant 0, Variant 1, Variant 2, Variant 3, and overlays the original-prompt estimate as a reference line with its own CIs -- i.e. no averaging over wordings before testing. (Separately, Figure A4 gives 5 more separate estimates: Base, No Scratch, No Transcripts, Other District, EEOC Guidance.) All are GPT-3.5 only; the 8-model main analysis in Figure 2 uses the single primary wording.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM (Fig. A3 caption): "Differences in mean model scores across variations in the wording of the prompt between synthetic applicants of different races and genders, reported in estimated population standard deviations, with 70% and 95% confidence intervals ... The blue vertical line represents the estimated effect in the original evaluation task, along with 70% and 95% confidence intervals." Axis row labels extracted from Fig. A3: "Variant 0 / Variant 1 / Variant 2 / Variant 3".

fields.value: Dispersion is shown graphically (per-variant point estimates with 70% and 95% CIs in Figures A3 and A4) and characterized qualitatively as small relative to estimation error, but NO numeric dispersion statistic is given -- no SD, range, min/max, or variance-component across wordings, and no point estimates are printed in text. The Figure A3 x-axis spans -0.05 to 0.15 population SD; the Figure A4 x-axis spans -0.05 to 0.20.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM: "We try four such variants, finding consistent but modestly variable race- and gender-effects with the rewritten prompts, as shown in Figure A3." and "As can be seen, estimated effects vary across conditions, but only slightly beyond what would be expected on the basis of estimation error alone." and (of Fig. A4) "the estimated race- and gender-effects vary modestly, but in many cases within the range we would expect from estimation error alone." No numeric across-wording dispersion appears; grep -ic 'variance' / 'standard deviation of' returns no such statistic.

fields.value: No placebo / null-edit arm. The manipulation is always demographic (name, title, pronouns, and race-linked indicia swapped simultaneously). The closest analogues are (a) a manipulation check that elicits the model's perceived race/gender of the synthetic applicant, and (b) a 'blinded' arm in which name/pronouns/other indicia are REMOVED -- neither is a semantically neutral edit holding the demographic signal fixed. The synthetic college is redrawn uniformly at random from 3 Texas universities independent of race/gender, but no same-group name-swap or neutral-edit contrast is estimated or reported.
fields.evidence: NEGATIVE SEARCHES on the extracted text: grep -ic 'placebo' = 0; 'null edit' = 0; 'control condition' = 0; 'same-race' = 0; 'within-group' = 0. Closest text, VERBATIM: "The college we list the synthetic applicant as having attended[d] is chosen uniformly at random from the following list, without regard to race or gender" -- a randomized nuisance factor, not a reported null-edit contrast.

fields.value: North Carolina statewide voter file (ncsbe.gov, cited by URL in a footnote). Procedure: random sample of 100,000 first and last names; each name embedded to 256 dimensions (512 total) with OpenAI text-embedding-small; a penalized logistic regression per race x gender cell predicts P(race, gender | embedding); names ranked by that probability, duplicate first names discarded; top 20 first+last name pairs retained per cell.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM: "To find names with this property, we draw real names from the North Carolina vote file, which is publicly available. Specifically, we choose a random sample of 100,000 first and last names, which we then embed into 256 dimensions (512 dimensions total) using OpenAI's text-embedding-small text embedding model. Then, for each of the eight possible choices of race and gender, we train a penalized logistic regression model to predict the probability that someone has the chosen race and gender using the embeddings." Footnote 1: "https://www.ncsbe.gov/results-data/voter-registration-data"

fields.value: 20 first+last name pairs per race x gender cell; 8 cells (Asian/Black/Hispanic/White x female/male) = 160 name pairs total, i.e. 40 per race collapsing over gender. One pair is drawn at random per synthetic dossier.
fields.evidence: VERBATIM: "we signal the applicant's race and gender through a random choice of one of twenty race- and gender-specific first- and last-name pairs" and "Finally, we choose the top twenty name pairs for each chosen race and gender."

fields.value: No name-level or per-name results. Names are treated as an interchangeable random draw within each race x gender cell; effects are estimated only at the group level, and clustering is on the real application dossier, not on the name. No leave-one-name-out, per-name spread, or name-as-random-effect analysis appears.
fields.evidence: NEGATIVE SEARCHES: grep -ic 'per-name' = 0; 'name-level' = 0; 'by name' = 0; 'individual name' = 0. Contrast VERBATIM: "errors are clustered at the level of the real application that was used to generate the synthetic application dossier" -- clustering unit is the dossier, and no name-indexed estimand is reported anywhere.

fields.value: Tokenization of the manipulated names is never discussed or controlled. Name selection is optimized purely for demographic signal strength (embedding-based P(race,gender) ranking); there is no matching or reporting on token count, name length, syllable count, string frequency, or population commonness.

fields.value: GPT-4 ranked the objectively STRONGER disability-enhanced CV first in only 15 of 60 ECVxCV trials, against a baseline in which identical CVs tied 70% of the time and no ECVxCV trial produced a tie at all. Per condition (ECV ranked 1st /10): Autism 0 (p<0.01), Deaf 1 (p<0.01), Depression 2 (p<0.05), Cerebral Palsy 2 (p<0.05), Blind 5 (n.s.), general Disability 5 (n.s.), all by one-tailed Fisher's exact vs. the CVxCV baseline error rate. Omnibus: Equal-Chance chi-square(6, N=60)=19.3, p<0.01; ECV-Better chi-square(6, N=60)=1971, p<0.001. Mitigation: the DEI/disability-justice-instructed custom GPT (DA-GPT) raised this to 37 of 60 (Mann-Whitney U, GPT-4 M=2.5 vs DA-GPT M=6.2, N=60, p<0.05), with significant per-condition gains only for Disability (10/10, p<0.05) and Deaf (9/10, p<0.05), and NO improvement for Depression (2/10 both arms). CAUTION on denominators: Table 4's total row gives 60 trials with 15 and 37; the body text writes the same two numbers as '15/70' and '37/70' (70 is the per-arm total INCLUDING the 10 baseline trials). The 60-trial denominator in Table 4 is the internally consistent one.
